sections.skill: Evaluate conclusions drawn from a line of fit

questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.skill: Evaluate conclusions drawn from a line of fit
questions.standard_level: Probability & Statistics. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Probability & Statistics, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: In a study of 7 volunteer students, each extra hour of study went with about 4 more points. Can a school claim this holds for all of its students? Explain.
questions.prompt_markup:
In a study of 7 volunteer students, each extra hour of study went with about 4 more points.
Can a school claim this holds for all of its students? Explain.
questions.correct_answer: Not with confidence: 7 volunteers are a small sample that was not randomly selected, and an observational study shows association, not cause.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation that names the sampling problem (small, not random) or the association-causation limit.

questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.skill: Evaluate conclusions drawn from a line of fit
questions.standard_level: Probability & Statistics. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Probability & Statistics, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: A study of 7 students who studied from 1 to 7 hours found the line ŷ = 4x + 58, where x is hours of study and ŷ is the test score out of 100. A report uses this line to predict a score of 138 for 20 hours of study. Why is that unreasonable?
questions.prompt_markup:
A study of 7 students who studied from 1 to 7 hours found the line ŷ = 4x + 58, where x is hours of study and ŷ is the test score out of 100.
A report uses this line to predict a score of 138 for 20 hours of study. Why is that unreasonable?
questions.correct_answer: 20 hours is far outside the data (1 to 7 hours), and the score cannot exceed 100.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation that names the extrapolation or the 100-point maximum.

sections.skill: Use a randomized experiment and simulation to test whether more study raises scores

questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.skill: Use a randomized experiment and simulation to test whether more study raises scores
questions.standard_level: Probability & Statistics. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Probability & Statistics, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: To test whether extra study raises scores, 40 volunteers were randomly assigned: 20 studied 3 extra hours and 20 did not. The extra-study group averaged 5 points higher. In 1,000 random regroupings of the 40 scores, a difference of 5 points or more (first group minus second) happened 18 times. Using a 5% threshold, is the difference significant? Explain.
questions.prompt_markup:
To test whether extra study raises scores, 40 volunteers were randomly assigned: 20 studied 3 extra hours and 20 did not. The extra-study group averaged 5 points higher. In 1,000 random regroupings of the 40 scores, a difference of 5 points or more (first group minus second) happened 18 times.
Using a 5% threshold, is the difference significant? Explain.
questions.correct_answer: Yes. 18 ÷ 1,000 = 1.8%, which is below 5%, so chance alone is unlikely to explain the difference; the extra study likely raised scores for volunteers like these.
questions.grading_note: Form required: the decision with the simulated proportion compared with 5%.

questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.skill: Use a randomized experiment and simulation to test whether more study raises scores
questions.standard_level: Probability & Statistics. Common Core groups high-school standards by category, not by course; this bank places this one in Probability & Statistics, following the Common Core traditional pathway (Appendix A) except where engine/hs_courses.py says otherwise.
questions.prompt: In a randomized experiment, a tutoring group averaged 6 points more than a control group. Random regroupings of the scores gave differences of 6 points or more 30% of the time. Using a 5% threshold, what is the conclusion?
questions.prompt_markup:
In a randomized experiment, a tutoring group averaged 6 points more than a control group. Random regroupings of the scores gave differences of 6 points or more 30% of the time.
Using a 5% threshold, what is the conclusion?
questions.correct_answer: The difference is not significant: 30% is above 5%, so it could easily be due to chance.
questions.grading_note: Form required: the conclusion with the comparison to 5%.

To remove the need for a control group
